item.title: Gas crisis puts mounting pressure on fuel oil
item.description:
Steel manufacturing company BSRM has kept production running with diesel and furnace oil amid the gas crisis, though output remains below half of its capacity. Due to the gas and electricity crisis, many other institutions across sectors, including pharmaceuticals and textiles, are following the same path. Multiple gas-dependent pharmaceutical factories in Pabna and Kaliakair, Gazipur, also relying on diesel to continue production.

The gas crisis is increasing pressure on fuel oil from two directions. Industries are using more diesel and furnace oil to run generators and boilers, while furnace-fired power plants are also consuming more fuel to offset electricity shortages. This information was obtained by analyzing the sales figures of the first 15 days of August from the three state-owned oil marketing companies—Padma Oil, Meghna Petroleum and Jamuna Oil.

Compared to the same period last year, Padma Oil's total diesel sales increased by nearly 29 per cent and furnace oil sales by 174 per cent in the first 15 days of this current August. Meghna Petroleum's diesel sales increased by nearly 21 per cent and furnace oil by 152 per centproductio. Jamuna Oil's diesel sales to industrial institutions increased by 33 per cent and furnace oil sales to industrial and power plants increased by 224 per cent.

Md. Mofizur Rahman, Managing Director of Padma Oil, told Prothom Alo that the demand for fuel oil from industrial factories has increased due to the gas crisis. The pressure is relatively higher in industrial belts around Dhaka, especially in Narayanganj and Gazipur. However, he said the situation is being managed.

The country’s industries had already been facing gas shortages but the crisis intensified after a fire accident at Excelerate Energy's floating liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal in Maheshkhali on 21 July. Under normal conditions, about 1 billion to 1.10 billion cubic feet of gas is added daily to the national grid from the two terminals in Maheshkhali. Following the accident, there was a major shortage in supply for about 25 days. The situation improved somewhat when Summit's terminal became fully operational and Excelerate's terminal became partially operational on 15 August.

However, that relief did not last because there was no new LNG cargo. Supply from Excelerate's terminal gradually decreased and came to a complete halt around 3:00 PM last Wednesday. Consequently, gas supply to the national grid dropped again, currently standing at around 2.22 billion cubic feet per day, whereas the country's demand is about 3.80 billion cubic feet.

This gas deficit is disrupting industrial production, with many institutions increasing their reliance on diesel and furnace oil to sustain production. Petrobangla has stated that the situation may improve when a new LNG cargo arrives tomorrow, on Sunday.

Use of oil is increasing in industries and power plants

In industrial factories, diesel is primarily used to run generators to generate electricity. In some cases, diesel is also used in boilers. Meanwhile, furnace oil is mainly used for generating heat in industrial boilers and furnaces. It is also used as fuel in furnace oil-fired power plants. Consequently, when gas and electricity shortages increase, the demand for both types of oil rises.

According to Padma Oil's calculations, 4,892 tons of diesel were sold to industrial institutions in the first 15 days of the current August. During the same period last year, it was 3,781 tons. This means diesel sales to industries increased by nearly 29 per cent.

The growth rate for furnace oil is even higher. Padma's sales to industries increased from 189 tons to 1,809 tons—a growth of nearly 857 per cent. However, in terms of volume, the vast majority went to power plants, where sales rose from 7,911 tons to 20,350 tons. Overall, Padma's furnace oil sales increased by nearly 174 per cent.

The pressure becomes clear just by looking at the sales figures of some of Padma's major industrial customers. Insepta Pharmaceuticals took 265.60 tons of diesel from Padma between 1 August to 15 August last year. During the same period this year, the company took 443.93 tons. This means their diesel intake increased by nearly 67 per cent.

Bengal Glass took 22.77 tons of diesel in the first 15 days of last year. This time, during the same period, it purchased 53.12 tons. That means diesel intake more than doubled, with a growth rate of nearly 133 per cent.

AKM Knitwear of the Al-Muslim Group took 37.94 tons of diesel during the same period last year. This time it took 113.83 tons, meaning the institution's diesel intake increased by 200 per cent.

A major increase was also seen in the case of Acme Laboratories. In the first 15 days of August last year, the company took 68.30 tons of diesel. This time it purchased 276.98 tons, meaning diesel intake increased by nearly 306 per cent. The Jamuna Group purchased 15.18 tons of diesel during the same period last year. This time it took 68.30 tons, with a growth rate of 350 per cent.

Eskayef Pharmaceuticals had purchased only 7.59 tons of diesel in the first 15 days of last year. This time, during the same period, it took 60.71 tons, meaning the institution's diesel intake increased by 700 per cent.

Far East Knitting and Dyeing Industries did not take any diesel from Padma during the same period last year. This time the company took 83.47 tons. Similarly, Crown Wears (Private) Limited did not take any diesel during that period last year, but this time took 75.89 tons.

Over two hundred factories are taking extra oil

Three oil company officials told Prothom Alo that more than 500 industrial factories, both small and large, regularly buy oil from the three companies. Compared to last year, 40 to 50 per cent of the factories are taking extra diesel and furnace oil.

Diesel sales by Meghna Petroleum to industrial customers increased from 7,122 tons to 11,722 tons—a growth of nearly 65 per cent. Over the same period, the company's total diesel sales increased by nearly 21 per cent. Furnace oil sales to industrial customers of this company increased from 236 tons to 623 tons.

However, the major pressure came from power plants, where furnace oil sales rose from 7,637 tons to 19,236 tons. As a result, the company's total furnace oil sales increased by nearly 152 per cent.

When asked, Md. Shahirul Hasan, Managing Director of Meghna Petroleum, said that although extra demand has come from industrial institutions, supply remains normal. This extra demand is relatively higher in the Dhaka region, especially with the demand for oil increasing from industrial institutions.

On the other hand, Jamuna Oil's diesel sales to industrial customers increased from 4,928 tons to 6,564 tons. Furthermore, combined furnace oil sales to industries and power plants rose from 3,989 tons to 12,928 tons.

Extra sales in BPC calculations

The same trend was observed in the data of the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation (BPC). In the first 15 days of the current August, 179,538 tons of diesel were sold in the country, with a daily average of about 11,969 tons. This is about 22 per cent higher than the daily average for the entirety of August last year.

Over the same period, 66,688 tons of furnace oil were sold, with a daily average of about 4,446 tons, which is about 76 per cent higher than the daily average for the entirety of August last year.

When asked, BPC Chairman Md. Manzur Alam Pradhan told Prothom Alo that although extra demand for fuel oil has come in, there is no shortage in reserves. The import process is normal, and regular oil tankers are arriving. According to BPC's figures for 15 August, the deliverable reserves of diesel in the country stood at 349,882 tons and furnace oil at 51,348 tons.

Production costs are rising due to oil

Although industrial institutions are sustaining production by using extra oil, their costs are increasing. Tapan Sengupta, Deputy Managing Director of BSRM, told Prothom Alo that after gas supplies were shut off, they had to use diesel and furnace oil. Their oil usage has increased by up to 70 per cent, raising their production costs at least fourfold.

The pharmaceutical industry faces the same pressure. Md. Zakir Hossain, former secretary general of the Bangladesh Association of Pharmaceutical Industries and managing director of Delta Pharma, told Prothom Alo that electricity from the national grid costs them about Tk 15 per unit.

Generating the same electricity with a diesel generator costs Tk 41 to 42. According to his calculations, overall energy costs are increasing by 75 to 80 per cent. Added to this are generator maintenance costs and losses from reduced production.

Running generators for long periods also requires more frequent servicing. Moreover, in sensitive production like pharmaceuticals, power outages sometimes require entire batches to be discarded.

item.title: Energy, work order deficits shut 457 factories down in 2 years
item.description:
A severe convergence of acute natural gas and electricity deficits, declining global export orders, mounting debt service pressures, and labor unrest has triggered widespread closures and worker retrenchments across Bangladesh’s core industrial belts.
Data compiled through August 2026 across Industrial Police records, trade body figures from BGMEA and BKMEA, and field reports reveals a systemic contraction operating on two distinct tracks: permanent factory closures that wipe out tens of thousands of jobs, and indefinite furloughs or operational slowdowns that leave hundreds of thousands of workers in economic limbo.
A total of 457 industrial units permanently closed across seven primary industrial zones.
This includes 108 BGMEA, 35 BKMEA, 8 BTMA, and 19 Bepza export-oriented plants, along with 287 non-apparel manufacturing units.
Between January and August 2026, 95 factories permanently shut down across three major industrial belts (Gazipur, Savar–Ashulia, and Narayanganj–Narsingdi), resulting in 61,881 direct job losses.
Gazipur alone accounted for 54 of these closures and 45,732 lost jobs.
Analysis of H1 2026 data shows 27 member factories permanently ceased operations, contributing to 19,188 workers being laid off or retrenched across 80 affiliated plants.
Acute gas pressure drops (often reaching zero to minimal PSI) forced short-term closures or extended leaves across 700 to 800 factories in Gazipur in early August, alongside 99 gas-dependent plants in Bhaluka (Mymensingh) operating at sub-50% capacity.

item.title: Low pressure forms in Bay of Bengal, signal No 3 at four ports
item.description:
A low-pressure system has formed over the northwest Bay of Bengal and adjoining coastal areas, prompting the Bangladesh Meteorological Department to issue a warning for four seaports.
The department said the low-pressure system could cause gusty or squally winds over the seaports, the north Bay and adjoining coastal areas of Bangladesh.
In a marine warning signed by meteorologist Md Toriful Newaz Kabir on Sunday, the seaports of Chittagong, Cox’s Bazar, Mongla and Payra were advised to hoist local warning signal No 3.
Fishing boats and trawlers in the north Bay have been advised to proceed towards the coast with caution until further notice.
Meanwhile, in its forecast for inland river ports from 9:30am to 6pm on Sunday, the Meteorological Department said wind speeds of 45-60kmph could occur over Khulna, Barisal, Patuakhali, Noakhali, Chittagong and Cox’s Bazar regions from the south or southeast.
Temporary rain or thundershowers, accompanied by gusty winds or squalls, are also likely in these areas.
River ports in the affected areas have been advised to hoist warning signal No 1.

item.title: Iran warns any country joining US sanctions considered “enemy”
item.description:
Iran on Saturday warned countries against participating in the United States' "economic war" against the Islamic republic, saying they would be considered enemies.

Washington has pushed its allies to jump aboard Donald Trump's new campaign to isolate the Iranian economy, as the US President's unpopular war drags toward the six-month mark.

"We declare to all countries... do not join the economic war waged by the United States," said Mohsen Rezai, the head of Iran's supreme national security council, on state television.

"Any country participating in the imposition of economic restrictions against us is considered an enemy," he added.

If the countries concerned refused to "distance themselves" from the United States, Iran would "harm" their interests, he added.

Rezai also insisted that the Islamic republic had more cards to play in the war, claiming that "we have not yet attacked any American economic interests".

"So far, we have only targeted military bases, but if they want to impose economic sanctions on us, the United States has oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere, and we will strike them," Rezai threatened.

Should Trump "take action, our confrontation will be like an earthquake", he added.

Washington has also called on other governments to join its efforts to isolate the Iranian economy, notably Beijing, among Iran's top strategic partners.

But China has criticised the initiative, arguing that American sanctions would not resolve the conflict in the Middle East.

One of Iran's major trading partners, the United Arab Emirates, announced on Tuesday that it was suspending all trade and financial transactions with Tehran until further notice.

Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 933 as three more die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three children died with measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours until 8:00am on Sunday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 933 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all three latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.
With these, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 834, while confirmed deaths from measles have remained the same at 99.
A total of 1,097 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, bringing the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 149,503.
Meanwhile, 131 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, bringing the total number of laboratory-confirmed infections to 18,404.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 130,609 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 125,975 have recovered, according to DGHS data.

Minister: HSIA 3rd terminal soft opening on Dec 16
item.description:
Newly appointed Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat on Sunday said the government is working to hold the soft opening of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport’s (HSIA) Third Terminal on December 16.
Speaking to journalists at his office at Bangladesh Secretariat on his first day in office, Millat outlined the government’s priorities for the aviation sector, including operationalizing the Third Terminal, resuming Dhaka-New York flights, expanding Biman Bangladesh Airlines’ fleet and advancing airport development projects.
He said steps are being taken to sign an agreement with a Japanese company in September in connection with the Third Terminal.
The government is also working to launch Dhaka-New York flights next year, while Millat expressed optimism that 10 leased aircraft could soon be added to Biman’s fleet.
Regarding Ishwardi Airport, he said the government is considering resuming flight operations soon to facilitate the transportation of radioactive materials for the nuclear power plant in Pabna.
On Jessore Airport, Millat said he had spoken with US-Bangla Airlines regarding flight operations following a decline in commercial flights at the airport.
He said a feasibility study for Bogra Airport is underway, while the government is hopeful of commissioning Cox’s Bazar International Airport in October.
Earlier in the morning, Millat formally joined the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism and was received by officials and employees with flowers. He later attended an exchange-of-views meeting with officials of the ministry and its departments.
Addressing the officials, Millat said his first priority would be to remove coordination gaps between the ministry and its departments and build an effective team to inject greater momentum into the aviation and tourism sectors.
“I am grateful to Honorable Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for entrusting me with the responsibility of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism. Reshuffling is a normal process. Under the new leadership, we want to move the ministry’s activities forward by building a team,” he said.
For greater efficiency and coordination, Millat said he intends to work from either the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) or Biman Bangladesh Airlines office one day in every five working days.
“My first task will be to eliminate the lack of coordination between the ministry and its departments,” he said.
He told officials that good performance would be rewarded while poor performance would face consequences, stressing that they must move beyond “conventional bureaucracy” to make the ministry’s activities more dynamic.
He also underscored the need for innovative planning to move the aviation and tourism sectors forward.

item.title: Law minister: Myanmar must take steps to protect Rohingya rights
item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman on Sunday said Myanmar government must take action to protect the human rights of its nationals, Rohingya people.
“Just as the Rohingya issue is viewed internationally, we also see it as an internal problem of Myanmar. The Rohingyas are citizens, a community and people of Myanmar. It is the Myanmar government that ultimately must take steps to protect their human rights,” he said.
The minister made the remarks at a discussion titled "Rohingya issue: present reality and future course of action" arranged by the Centre for Policy Research at the Jatiya Press Club in the city.
He said the Ziaur Rahman and Khaleda Zia’s governments successfully addressed the Rohingya issue and tried to convince Myanmar that the Rohingya people are an integral part of its territory at different times.
But the successive governments couldn’t address the Rohingya issue in the same way, he added.
The law minister said Bangladesh needs to build national unity alongside securing international support to resolve the Rohingya crisis.
Referring to the keynote speaker’s observation that Bangladesh needs to convince the United States, China and India about the Rohingya issue, he said discussions with those countries are certainly necessary, but Bangladeshis must first stand united.
“Before convincing others, the people of Bangladesh must stand together. Irrespective of political affiliations and differences of opinion, we must understand that this land, this Bangladesh, should come first,” he said.
Asaduzzaman said Bangladesh provided shelter to the displaced Rohingyas on humanitarian grounds.
“We believe the Rohingya crisis is, on the one hand, an internal crisis of Myanmar, while on the other, the Bangladesh government provided shelter to them and stood by them on humanitarian grounds,” he said, adding that Bangladesh also has a moral responsibility to stand by them under Article 25 of the Constitution.
The Rohingyas are culturally and ethnically inhabitants of Myanmar territory and are entitled to certain protections there under international law. “So, we support addressing the issue from that perspective and on that basis,” he said.
Former Bangladesh ambassador to Myanmar Mohammad Sufiur Rahman presented the keynote in the discussion, while Executive Director of the Center for Policy Research Dr Shafiqul Islam and its trustee member Prof Sk Tawfique M Haque and Rohingya women's rights activist Razia Sultana, among others, spoke on the occasion.

item.title: Iran warns any country joining US sanctions considered 'enemy'
item.description:
Iran on Saturday warned countries against participating in the United States’ “economic war” against the Islamic republic, saying they would be considered enemies.
Washington has pushed its allies to jump aboard Donald Trump’s new campaign to isolate the Iranian economy as the US president's unpopular war drags toward the six-month mark.
“We declare to all countries... do not join the economic war waged by the United States,” said Mohsen Rezai, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, on state television.
“Any country participating in the imposition of economic restrictions against us is considered an enemy,” he added.
If the countries concerned refused to “distance themselves” from the United States, Iran would “harm” their interests, he added.
Rezai also insisted that the Islamic republic had more cards to play in the war, claiming that “we have not yet attacked any American economic interests."
“So far, we have only targeted military bases, but if they want to impose economic sanctions on us, the United States has oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere, and we will strike them,” Rezai threatened.
Should Trump “take action, our confrontation will be like an earthquake," he added.
Washington has also called on other governments to join its efforts to isolate the Iranian economy, notably Beijing, among Iran’s top strategic partners.
But China has criticized the initiative, arguing that American sanctions would not resolve the conflict in the Middle East.
One of Iran’s major trading partners, the United Arab Emirates, announced on Tuesday that it was suspending all trade and financial transactions with Tehran until further notice.

item.title: Canada retaliates as trade war with US escalates
item.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced retaliatory tariffs on the United States on Saturday after walking away from a “bad deal” on trade in a deepening rift between the longtime allies.
Negotiations between the neighboring countries broke down Friday in Washington, putting into force new 50% US tariffs impacting about $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5% of Canadian exports to the United States. Impacted products range from hockey sticks to cement.
“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said.
US President Donald Trump hit back at Canada on Sunday, saying, “Canada wants the benefits of being a state without being one!!!”
“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs. No more!!!” Trump added in a post on Truth Social.
New Canadian tariffs will notably target the US steel and dairy industries and take effect on September 8. More details would come next week, Carney said.
Trump had previously said Washington “should be able to have a deal with Canada,” citing his “good relationship” with Carney.
But on Saturday, Canada’s prime minister said Trump set conditions that were ultimately unacceptable even though earlier talks had been positive.
“In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic and unfair and undermined the net benefits for Canada and called into question the reliability of any deal,” Carney said in Ottawa.
“We cannot accept what they’ve offered, and we will not give what they’ve asked.”
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told the New York Times on Saturday that the US had offered to reduce its tariffs on steel, aluminum, and autos, as well as eliminate a recently imposed tariff on Canadian lumber.
Greer said those measures would have given Canada “the most preferential treatment of any trading partner,” according to the Times.
Greer told Fox News on Saturday that Washington was “moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation.” He said no new talks were planned with Canadian negotiators.
A senior US official characterized this week’s talks in Washington as candid and not acrimonious.
Canada has been seeking relief from Trump’s tariffs on autos, steel, and aluminum, which have battered the country’s economy, forced job losses, and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.
The White House had alleged “discriminatory treatment” by Canada against US alcohol, automobile, and dairy products in introducing the duties.
They were originally set to take effect on Wednesday, before Trump issued a three-day reprieve citing progress in talks.
Carney said one reason the deal collapsed was US negotiators at the 11th hour introducing restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries.
US negotiators also made unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture,” he said, referring to the French-speaking province in eastern Canada.
The escalating trade war was met with anger by Democratic lawmakers and governors from border states, including Minnesota, New York, and Washington, who blamed Trump for triggering chaos that will raise costs on US businesses and families.
“Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That’s Trump’s economic policy in a nutshell,” New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted on X.
Beyond the latest tariffs, the US and Canada still have to agree on revisions to the North American free trade agreement, USMCA, which Trump declined to renew in its current form.
Trump’s threats to make Canada the 51st US state have also antagonized Canadians.
Carney has repeatedly said relations with the US have been forever altered and that Canada must reduce reliance on its southern neighbor, which currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports.
“We’ve been under no illusions. We recognized from the start that America has changed,” Carney said Saturday. “We recognize that sometimes, its signature was written in pencil.”
Carney spoke with provincial leaders to outline next steps.
One of them, Ontario Premier Doug Ford, said Canadians must remain united.
Trump “can’t be trusted, simple as that,” Ford told reporters. “President Trump is the type of person who would steal your lunch money.”
The Business Roundtable, a group of 200 chief executives of leading US corporations, warned the new tariffs “risk raising costs for American businesses and families" and urged both governments to resume negotiations.

item.title: LGRD minister: Local govt elections to be held on time
item.description:
Local government elections will be held on time by strictly following constitutional procedures and rules, newly appointed Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Minister Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan said on Sunday.
“Elections would be held at all five tiers of local government, with the government expecting genuine representatives of the people to be elected,” he said.
The minister made the remarks while exchanging views with officials of the ministry and its subordinate agencies at the Secretariat on his first working day after assuming office.
Asked when local government elections would begin and whether they would be completed within a year, Moyeen Khan said there was a constitutional process for holding the elections and that it would not be appropriate for him to announce a specific date without following that process.
“Following the constitutional process and observing all the rules, the BNP government will announce the local government elections at the appropriate time,” he said.
The minister said holding local government elections within a particular timeframe was not his personal target but a government objective aimed at reflecting the will of the people.
He stressed that local government elections were not limited to city corporations.
“There are elections at different tiers of local government. Elections will be held at all five tiers, and our expectation is that genuine representatives of the people will be elected,” he said.
Noting that the elections of 2008, 2014, 2018 and 2024 had failed to reflect the will of the people, the minister said he considered the February 12, 2026 election an opportunity through which genuine representatives of the people had come before the country.
The minister also described the Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Ministry as different from many other ministries because of its direct and day-to-day engagement with citizens.
“The main objective of the government is to serve the people, and this ministry is among those that work directly with the people every day, 365 days a year,” he said.
Moyeen Khan said local government was an important component of the democratic system and that the effective functioning of the ministry would contribute to the overall functioning of the government and the country.
He said the ministry worked directly with people at the grassroots and pledged to ensure that government policies and services reached them effectively.
The minister said the government would succeed when services were properly delivered to people at the grassroots.
He said the government would serve all citizens, but special attention would be given to poor, disadvantaged and underprivileged people.
“Those who are affluent and wealthy are less dependent on government support because they can manage many of their own needs. But poor people need greater assistance from the government,” he said.
According to estimates, around 40 percent of Bangladesh’s population still lives in poverty in one form or another, he said, adding that the rights of poor people had been deprived during the previous government. He also highlighted the Family Card and Farmer Card programs introduced by BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman.
He said his focus would remain on addressing the needs of disadvantaged people and that he wanted to work alongside citizens, standing with them, to serve the country under the responsibility entrusted to him by the prime minister.

item.title: India seeks new charge on electricity exports to Bangladesh
item.description:
Bangladesh regularly imports electricity from India. India has now sought to impose a new charge on the electricity it exports to Bangladesh, demanding 0.005 Indian rupees per unit. If the charge is added, the cost of imported electricity will increase.

However, delays in reaching an agreement over the charge could disrupt electricity imports from India.

The Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources has sought the Finance Ministry’s opinion on signing a new agreement. In a letter sent to the Finance Division on 18 August, the Power Division said a Settlement Nodal Agency (SNA) agreement needs to be signed between the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) and NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam Ltd (NVVN), an Indian state-owned company.

Any delay in signing the agreement could create complications in importing 1,160 megawatts of electricity through NVVN, it said.

According to the letter, India’s Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) initially proposed a charge of 0.01 Indian rupees per unit for cross-border electricity trade. Following an application by BPDB, the charge was later reduced by half to 0.005 rupees.

Officials from the Power Division and BPDB said the SNA charge is not part of the price of electricity; rather, it covers the cost of grid operations and settlement of cross-border electricity transactions. As a result, the additional cost will not be significant, they said.

They also said signing the agreement with NVVN would simplify transactions, as there would no longer be a need to settle bills separately with individual power plants.

The Power Division’s letter said CERC introduced the SNA system to simplify the settlement of grid-related charges in electricity trade with neighbouring countries. The same SNA charge is also being levied on electricity traded between India and Nepal and Bhutan.

According to BPDB sources, India has proposed the charge to cover the costs of scheduling the amount of electricity to be supplied at different times, collecting consumption data from meters, reconciling supply and consumption figures, and operating the grid.

Bangladesh currently has agreements allowing it to import a total of 2,656MW of electricity from India under several contracts. Of this, government-level arrangements through NVVN include 250MW from an NTPC power plant, 300MW from Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) and 160MW from the Tripura State Electricity Corporation.

In addition, Bangladesh has agreements to import 200MW from a power plant of Sembcorp Energy India through PTC India and another 250MW directly from Sembcorp. The initiative to sign an SNA agreement between NVVN and BPDB covers a total of 1,160MW.

Separately, Bangladesh has an agreement to import 1,496MW from the Adani power plant in Godda, Jharkhand. BPDB officials said the power purchase agreement with Adani already includes provisions for such charges, so a separate SNA agreement will not be required for that electricity.

item.title: Tenders fail to secure enough LNG amid gas crisis
item.description:
The government is struggling to secure liquefied natural gas (LNG) as none of the cargoes ordered through the direct procurement method (DPM) have arrived. With LNG unavailable as needed, the government has had to buy cargoes at higher prices in emergency tenders, increasing the cost of one cargo by at least Tk 1.65 billion.

Petrobangla oversees LNG imports with approval from the Energy Division, while its subsidiary Rupantarita Prakritik Gas Company Ltd (RPGCL) is responsible for importing the fuel.

Three officials involved in LNG supply told Prothom Alo that LNG prices are rising with every tender. They said LNG could have been purchased at lower prices had tenders been invited earlier instead of using the DPM.

According to Petrobangla and RPGCL sources, tenders were invited on 17 August to purchase three LNG cargoes for August and two for the first week of September. British Petroleum (BP) emerged as the lowest bidder for two cargoes, quoting less than USD 22 per unit.

A second tender was called on 18 August for three more cargoes, with Saudi Aramco emerging as the lowest bidder for the 1–2 September cargo at below USD 24.

In a third tender on 19 August, BP offered USD 25.31 for the 26–27 August cargo. The government decided not to buy the 29–30 August cargo because bids were even higher.

The government had earlier approved direct purchases of several cargoes in an effort to secure LNG at lower prices. Four of those cargoes were scheduled to arrive in August, but none has arrived. This has created a shortfall in gas supply, forcing the government to buy LNG at higher prices.

Officials involved in LNG imports said every USD 1 increase in the price of LNG per unit costs the government an additional Tk 413.3 million. As much as USD 4 more per unit has had to be paid for an emergency cargo, meaning the additional cost for one cargo is at least Tk 1.65 billion.

Petrobangla Chairman Md Abdul Mannan told Prothom Alo that LNG supply has increased compared with earlier and efforts are being made to maintain supply with the amount available. The government is also trying to bring in LNG under long- and short-term contracts, he said.

Terminals ready, but LNG is in short supply

Domestic gas production has been declining for nine years, prompting Bangladesh to begin importing LNG in 2018. Two floating LNG terminals operate at Maheshkhali—one owned by US company Excelerate Energy and the other by local company Summit. Excelerate’s terminal was shut down after a fire on 21 July.

Excelerate’s terminal has a daily capacity of 600 million cubic feet, while Summit’s can handle 500 million cubic feet. Together, they could supply up to 1.05 billion cubic feet a day.

Bangladesh imported 11 LNG cargoes in July through long- and short-term contracts and the spot market. In August, nine cargoes were expected, but only four have arrived.

One came from Qatar under a long-term contract, while an LNG cargo from Saudi Aramco under a short-term deal could not be unloaded because it was not suitable for transfer.

None of the four cargoes purchased directly arrived. As a result, the government bought an emergency cargo at a higher price. It reached the Bay of Bengal on 22 August, and Excelerate’s terminal resumed supplying gas to the pipeline that afternoon.

Gas supply has since increased, but it is being kept limited because there is no certainty about when the next LNG cargo will arrive. As a result, the gas crisis may take more time to ease fully.

According to Petrobangla, daily gas demand is around 3.8 billion cubic feet, while the maximum supply has been about 2.7 billion cubic feet. LNG normally accounts for 1.05 billion cubic feet of that supply, with the rest coming from domestic gas fields. LNG supply has averaged only about half of terminal capacity over the past month. On Saturday, supply increased somewhat, reaching 750 million cubic feet on Sunday evening. Total gas supply was 2.38 billion cubic feet.

Bangladesh normally imports LNG through long-term contracts and tenders. The government has long-term contracts with Qatar and Oman, but LNG shipments from the two countries have virtually stopped since the war began in the Middle East, with only occasional cargoes arriving. Bangladesh also has a short-term contract with Saudi Aramco and regularly purchases LNG from the spot market through tenders based on demand.

Officials said the situation in the Middle East remains uncertain, while European countries are building up LNG stocks ahead of winter. With a global shortage of LNG cargoes, securing supplies could remain difficult despite repeated tenders.

Energy expert M Tamim told Prothom Alo that global energy market volatility could ease if the war ends completely. For now, the government needs to prioritise gas supply, he said. It could increase power generation using fuel oil and divert more gas to industries.

“Bangladesh cannot afford to buy LNG at the current high prices,” Tamim said, adding that the government needs to make decisions that are not merely economic but also political.

item.title: CPD: 6 months after polls, negative trends still overshadow economic recovery
item.description:
While the new government's first six months show some positive changes, negative trends still dominate the path to economic recovery, according to the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD).
The think tank noted that despite minor improvements in inflation and foreign exchange reserves, deep concerns persist over revenue collection, investment, industrial production, employment, and the energy sector.
At a media dialogue in the capital on Monday, CPD distinguished fellow Dr Debapriya Bhattacharya stated that the performance presents a mixed picture tilted heavily toward negative trends, with most of these challenges being structural in nature.
Debapriya highlighted that the 6-month evaluation analyzed 362 observations across nine sectors: governance and administration, public finance management, industry and trade, banking and financial services, energy and transport, agriculture, education, health, and social protection.
The evaluation exclusively focused on actionable steps taken rather than mere announcements.
CPD's analysis showed headline inflation dropping from 9.1% to 8.3% between February and July, while food inflation eased from 9.3% to 7.2%.
However, pressure on ordinary citizens remains severe due to the high prices of essential commodities.
Furthermore, real wage growth remains negative, meaning the dip in inflation has not translated into the expected boost in purchasing power.
Concerns over revenue, investment, and industry
CPD identified weak tax collection as a primary bottleneck in economic recovery efforts.
Total tax revenue growth decelerated from 12.3% to 4.9% between March and May.
They warned that meeting the revenue target for the current fiscal year will be difficult, forecasting a potential revenue shortfall of nearly Tk130,000 crore to Tk140,000 crore in FY27.
However, CPD advised the government to safeguard allocations for education, health, and social safety nets.
Investment figures remain equally disappointing. Private sector credit growth slowed from 6% to 4.5% between February and June, while letter of credit (LC) openings for capital machinery fell into negative territory. Net foreign direct investment (FDI) also declined—signaling no clear path toward a swift private investment rebound.
The ongoing gas crisis was highlighted as a major risk factor.
Technical glitches at the Maheshkhali LNG terminal, complications in procuring spot-market LNG cargoes, and weak supply planning severely hit gas-dependent industries, including textiles, steel, paper, particle board, and ceramics.
During March–April, growth in both the general index of industrial production and the manufacturing sector index ground to zero. Gas consumption within the industrial sector also contracted.
To address this, CPD recommended time-bound domestic gas exploration, strategic fuel reserves, source diversification, and a review of power purchase agreements (PPAs) to ease subsidy burdens.
Banking sector reforms initiated
CPD acknowledged a few positive regulatory steps, such as the decision to merge five troubled Islamic banks and applying the Bank Resolution Act to failing financial institutions.
However, lingering concerns remain regarding the independence of Bangladesh Bank, top-level leadership appointments, and structural reforms. CPD emphasized that restoring confidence requires a comprehensive structural roadmap.
The external sector offers a mixed picture.
Gross foreign reserves calculated under BPM6 rose from $30.1 billion to $32.3 billion between February 19 and August 12.
However, the trade deficit widened, the current account shifted from surplus into deficit, and growth in remittances and overseas employment slowed—impacted significantly by ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
Why Recovery Is Lagging
Dr Debapriya outlined key reasons for the sluggish recovery:
CPD stressed that economic recovery cannot be defined solely by lower inflation; it demands stability across exchange and interest rates alongside visible gains in GDP growth, private investment, and job creation.
To support sustained recovery, CPD advised preparing a realistic core budget for the October–June period built on real-time data and credible fiscal parameters.
It called for an integrated reform package covering energy, banking, revenue administration, development expenditure rationalization, security, supply chain management, and digitalization—backed by effective inter-institutional coordination and regular parliamentary accountability.
CPD concluded that while the government took several reformative and welfare-oriented steps during its first six months, core structural vulnerabilities remain unaddressed.
Moving forward, substituting isolated measures with an integrated, realistic, and accountable reform program represents the government's single biggest challenge.

item.title: New govt pay structure: Delay in decision will complicate situation: Debapriya Bhattacharya
item.description:
Debapriya Bhattacharya, distinguished fellow of the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) and convener of the Citizen’s Platform for SDG Implementation, believes the government lacks the political courage to introduce a new pay structure for government employees.

He said keeping the issue pending will not reduce the problem; rather, the situation will become more complicated the longer the government delays taking a decision.

Debapriya Bhattacharya made the remarks at a media dialogue organised by CPD on the government’s six-month performance at CPD’s office in the capital’s Dhanmondi on Monday.

CPD’s another distinguished fellow Mustafizur Rahman and additional research director Toufiq-ul Islam Khan were also present.

Debapriya Bhattacharya said, “Even after six months, you have not been able to take a decision on pay and allowances. Why can’t you? There is a major issue, which is financial capacity. There will be a shortfall of Tk 1.4 trillion from the revenue collection target of Tk 6.95 trillion for the current fiscal year.”

Debapriya Bhattacharya further said, “The interim government had left a report on the pay structure, and after evaluating it, a recommendation was made to implement the pay structure in phases, which everyone had also agreed to. Instead of delaying so much, if you had initially provided a 20–25 per cent dearness allowance and asked for some time, that would have been very good. The situation has now been brought to a point that is not good.”

Debapriya Bhattacharya believes keeping the issue pending will not reduce the problem; rather, the situation will become more complicated the longer the government delays. According to him, delays in taking a decision on pay and allowances will also disrupt the government’s other activities.

62,000 people lost jobs

Regarding the government’s six-month performance, CPD said 95 factories in the country’s three major industrial zones have permanently closed between January and August this year. As a result, 61,881 people have lost their jobs.

Debapriya Bhattacharya said the government inherited some structural difficulties when it took office. The global situation was also not favourable at the time. War broke out. The problem is that the government did not prepare a comprehensive document on the situation it inherited when it assumed responsibility. As a result, it is now difficult to assess various measures and economic progress, he said.

He said the government has repeatedly stated that it took charge amid a difficult situation. But no comprehensive, data-based document was prepared on the situation from which the government took responsibility. As a result, it has now become difficult to reconcile the government’s various statements with statistics, he said.

Mentioning that there were two major expectations from the new government—economic recovery and establishing good governance—Debapriya Bhattacharya said some discomfort has emerged in these areas.

No comprehensive action plan has been seen for the reform programme. Many of the commissions mentioned in the manifesto have also not been implemented, he added.

Debapriya said CPD has prepared a list of around 362 measures to assess the new government’s promises and various steps it has taken. These have been divided into nine categories and are being evaluated under the 'Reform Tracker'.

For good governance, 105 incidents have been included in the assessment. The decision by government MPs not to take plots and cars, the speedy trial of the Ramisa murder case and the initiative to bring discipline to the transport system using artificial intelligence were mentioned as positive measures.

On the other hand, CPD considers the appointment of politically affiliated individuals to senior positions a matter of concern. Debapriya also said the government has deviated from its commitment to making appointments based on merit.

item.title: Reopening border haats, lifting restrictions on yarn imports discussed with Indian envoy
item.description:
Bangladesh’s Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir and Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi discussed several issues aimed at further strengthening trade relations between Bangladesh and India.

According to a statement from the Commerce Ministry, the two sides discussed reopening the border haats that have remained closed, making the land ports fully operational and lifting restrictions on the import of yarn through land routes.

The issues were discussed at a meeting between Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir and Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi at the Secretariat on Monday.

The meeting also covered expanding bilateral trade, removing trade barriers, promoting joint investment and increasing cooperation between businesses of the two countries.

After the meeting, the commerce minister said bilateral trade between Bangladesh and India currently stands at around USD 13 billion. However, trade has slowed somewhat over the past one and a half years due to various obstacles. The meeting focused on identifying these problems and discussing ways to make trade easier and more effective.

The commerce minister said India is Bangladesh’s second-largest trading partner after China and that the two countries have longstanding economic ties.

He said priority was given to bringing the land ports into full operation, reopening closed border haats and lifting restrictions on yarn imports by land to further strengthen economic relations.

The minister also said a proposal had been made to form a joint task force to enhance cooperation between businesses in the two countries.

The two sides also discussed creating new investment opportunities and making business communication easier through improvements in digital infrastructure.

Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi said that although Bangladesh and India have some differences on political and economic issues, their people want development and progress. The two countries need to work together, particularly for the future of their younger generations, he said.

Trivedi also said Bangladesh and India are independent and sovereign countries. Neither country is bigger or smaller than the other, and both are equal. Relations should move forward on the basis of this equality, he said.

The Indian high commissioner said economic cooperation is the most important factor in improving relations between the two countries. In his view, stronger economic ties would create opportunities for cooperation in other areas as well.

Emphasising joint investment and production, Trivedi said Bangladesh’s garment industry has been successful in global markets. India could support the sector by supplying zippers, machinery, buttons and other inputs, he said. This would further increase mutual dependence between the two countries.

Praising Bangladesh’s garments, he said he feels proud when he sees clothing labelled “Made in Bangladesh” in international markets. The country’s garment sector could expand further through joint initiatives between Bangladesh and India, he added.

The meeting also placed emphasis on increasing cooperation between businesses, creating new investment opportunities and strengthening supply chains. Both sides expressed hope that these initiatives would further strengthen trade relations between Bangladesh and India.

Cabinet approves draft Armed Police Battalions Act, 2026
item.description:
By UNB

The cabinet on Monday approved the draft of Armed Police Battalions Act, 2026, with a view to modernising and making the force more people-friendly by abolishing the existing ordinance.

The approval came from the cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Secretariat.

According to the proposed law, the Armed Police Battalion will be entrusted with responsibilities, including maintaining public security, providing security to VIPs and government-declared important installations, and taking action against those involved in terrorism, drug trafficking, human trafficking, rape and crimes against humanity.

The battalion, which is part of the police force, will also assist other law enforcement agencies in maintaining law and order.

The draft law also proposes empowering the members of the battalion to investigate criminal offences and conduct related proceedings, subject to compliance with the Code of Criminal Procedure and other laws.

It further proposes provisions for the establishment of special courts and summary courts and lays down procedures for conducting trials.

Under the proposed law, the Armed Police Battalion will operate under the control and supervision of an additional inspector general of police.

The draft law was prepared in Bangla, making the existing legal framework more up-to-date and the Armed Police Battalion more people-oriented.

The draft was uploaded on the website of the Ministry of Home Affairs to seek public opinion.

The proposed law seeks to repeal the Armed Police Battalions Ordinance, 1979, but retains the validity of actions taken under the existing ordinance.

The draft law was given final approval by the Cabinet subject to vetting by the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division.

By bdnews24.com

Bangladesh must pursue constitutional reforms while keeping the original Constitution of 1972 as the foundation, Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman has said.

Part A of Article 6 of the July Charter repeatedly says these measures have to be carried out through constitutional amendments, he explained.

“That means I have accepted the 1972 Constitution as the basis. Whatever I do, I have to move forward with the 1972 Constitution before me. That is one part of my July Charter.”

Asaduzzaman was speaking as chief guest at a dialogue titled “Post-election Bangladesh: Political Promises and Reality” at the CIRDAP auditorium in Dhaka on Monday.

The Centre for Governance Studies (CGS) organised the event with representatives of the government and political parties, lawyers, journalists, human rights activists and members of civil society.

CGS President Zillur Rahman moderated the discussion.

The law minister said those who had argued for discarding the 1972 Constitution altogether would have offered a simpler route.

“If we had done what those who said the 1972 Constitution should be thrown away wanted, I could have gone down a straight line,” he said.

“But as long as the 1972 Constitution remains, I have to amend that Constitution. In going through the amendment process, I have to keep before me the points of the July Charter that we signed for reform.”

July Charter Order Questioned

Asaduzzaman also questioned the “July Charter Implementation Order” issued during the interim administration, saying it was inconsistent with the Constitution.

Explaining why an “order” had been issued rather than an ordinance, he said: “If this amounts to something equivalent to amending the Constitution, then it conflicts with the Constitution.

“An ordinance cannot be issued if it is equivalent to a constitutional amendment. That is why they did not go for an ordinance and instead issued an order.”

He then questioned the legal status of that order.

“What is the legal status of this order? Under the Third Schedule of the Constitution, the power to issue such orders ceased from the day the Constitution came into operation in 1972.

“Some laws were made through presidential orders in 1972, and those have the status of law. But it was also made clear that after the Constitution came into force, the president would no longer have the power to issue such orders.”

Asaduzzaman said laws must be passed by parliament, while ordinances can be issued when parliament is not in session.

He argued that by issuing the July Charter implementation order, the interim government had left behind a “path to division”.

‘You Have the Right to Hold Programmes’

The law minister later responded to questions raised by political leaders who had spoken earlier in the discussion.

Didarul Alam Bhuiyan, joint general secretary of Rashtra Sanskar Andolan, said his party had sought permission to hold a rally at the Central Shaheed Minar last Saturday but was denied permission because a case had been filed against one of its members.

The law minister said there was no law that could justify such a restriction unless the party itself was banned.

“There is no such law as long as your political party is not regarded as a banned political entity,” he said.

“Since your party is not banned, you can organise programmes and criticise the government there. You certainly did not enter politics to sing the government’s praises.

“You have that right, and it is the government’s responsibility to ensure that right. I hope we will address these issues.”

Constitution Reform Committee

NCP Joint Convenor Monira Sharmin raised the issue of the parliamentary committee on constitutional reform.

The law minister said the plan had been to form a 17-strong committee during the first session of parliament, with seven members from the BNP, five from the opposition alliance, and five from other political parties.

“We asked the opposition to give us five names, but they said they would provide them in the next session,” he said.

“We held repeated meetings but did not receive the names. We have now formed a 12-member committee.

“I hope that if they submit the names, we can move forward with constitutional amendments along the path of reform. We will try to incorporate any of your proposals if they are reasonable.”

Freedom of Expression, Extrajudicial Killings

Law Minister Asaduzzaman also addressed freedom of expression and extrajudicial killings.

“We are trying to move away from that culture,” he said.

“We have turned around and are trying to reach the right destination. Our pace may be slow, but look at the statistics and see what the situation with extrajudicial killings has been over the past six months.”

He also spoke about the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Act enacted during the interim government.

“I was the attorney general at the time,” he said. “The attorney general is never involved in vetting legislation.”

He said the law provided for trials over enforced disappearances both at the International Crimes Tribunal and in ordinary courts, but did not clearly specify which cases should go before which jurisdiction.

It also provided for a maximum punishment without setting a minimum sentence, he said. “The law was placed before parliament to correct these anomalies.”

Asaduzzaman said the government was trying to build a system of accountability.

“We are putting it into practice and will see how successful we can be. If it does not work, we are open to amendments.

“A law is not the Quran or the Bible that cannot be changed.”

Law Minister’s Interim Role Criticised

Gono Forum President Subrata Chowdhury challenged Asaduzzaman over his criticism of the former interim government.

“We now criticise the interim government so much. But he, the current law minister, was one of its strongest supporters,” Subrata said.

“The interim government could hardly move forward without his advice, and it trusted him.

“After doing all these things on behalf of the interim government, he has now joined this government and says he does not have that much power. We saw then how much power you had.”

Jatiya Party Secretary General Shameem Haider Patwary said many figures associated with the “spirit of July” had gradually disappeared from the political scene.

“We have gradually seen many people who embodied the spirit of July disappear completely. Now the spirit of July itself is also disappearing,” he said.

He argued that judicial reform had been the most urgent element of the broader reform agenda.

Bangladesh JaSaD Presidium Member Mushtuq Husain said his party had not signed the July Charter and had opposed the referendum.

“A referendum should take place after constitutional amendments,” he said. “There was language there that openly sought to discard the 1972 Constitution.”

He also strongly criticised Ali Riaz, who headed the Constitution Reform Commission.

Questions Over Foreign Policy

Sohrab Hasan, editor of the news outlet Charcha, raised questions about the government’s current foreign policy.

“The ruling party is silent about the US trade agreement, and so is the opposition,” he said. “We do not know where the government is heading in foreign policy.

“When war was imposed on Iran, our foreign ministry issued a statement as though Iran itself was responsible for the war.”

Prime Minister’s Political Advisor Zahir Uddin Swapon blamed the current energy problems on what he described as the previous government’s “political legacy”.

He argued that the crisis could have been avoided if the previous government had focused on extracting domestic energy resources such as gas instead of pursuing an import-dependent policy.

item.title: Repatriation deadlock pushes Dhaka to rethink Rohingya policy
item.description:
Nine years after the mass Rohingya exodus into Bangladesh, hopes of returning home have faded into deepening uncertainty, with repatriation stalled, violence continuing in Myanmar’s Rakhine State and a worsening humanitarian crisis pushing growing numbers of refugees towards dangerous sea journeys.
More than 1.2 million Rohingya are now living in 32 camps in Ukhiya and Teknaf, nine years after hundreds of thousands fled Myanmar following the military crackdown that began on August 25, 2017.
The population has continued to grow, with 154,690 new arrivals registered between December 2024 and July this year.
For many refugees, the overriding wish remains unchanged: to return safely and with dignity to their homes in Rakhine.
But fighting between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army, which now controls much of Rakhine, has made prospects for repatriation even more remote.
The prolonged uncertainty is increasingly taking a human toll.
UN data cited by Save the Children shows the number of Rohingya attempting to flee Bangladesh and Myanmar by boat has risen 90% from last year.
At least 530 Rohingya who left for Malaysia in July aboard a smugglers’ vessel have remained missing for nearly three weeks.
The trend follows the deadliest year on record for Rohingya sea crossings.
Nearly 900 died or went missing in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2025, while more than 6,500 attempted the journey.
More than 2,800 had already taken to the sea between January and April 13 this year.
Bangladesh and Myanmar first signed a repatriation agreement in November 2017, followed by arrangements intended to complete returns within two years.
Yet not a single large-scale voluntary repatriation has materialised.
Attempts in 2018 and 2019 collapsed as refugees refused to return without guarantees over citizenship and security.
Myanmar says it has now verified 426,545 of the 828,824 names submitted by Bangladesh, identifying 388,797 as former residents of Rakhine. But verification has produced no timetable for their return.
The diplomatic dispute has meanwhile sharpened.
Myanmar recently rejected accounts of more than one million Rohingya being displaced into Bangladesh and again referred to them as “Bengalis”.
Dhaka formally rejected the terminology and disputed Myanmar’s statistics.
With bilateral repatriation effectively stalled, Bangladesh is increasingly seeking a broader political solution involving Asean, China, Turkey, Malaysia, Norway and other international partners, while pushing for guarantees of citizenship, security and dignified return.
UNHCR spokesperson Shari Yasmin Nijman said conditions inside Myanmar remain unsuitable for voluntary, safe and sustainable repatriation.
“Ultimately, the solution to this crisis lies with Myanmar,” she said, stressing that any return must be voluntary, informed, safe and dignified.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam echoed that position, saying refugee camps could never become a permanent substitute for a homeland.
“The Rohingya crisis originated in Myanmar, and its sustainable solution must ultimately be found in Myanmar,” she said, calling safe, voluntary and dignified return “the only sustainable path”.
Former ambassador M Humayun Kabir said there was no way to predict how much longer the crisis would continue.
“It will depend on political will,” he said. “If there is political will, it is possible in a shorter time.”
Nine years after the exodus, that political will remains elusive.
For more than a million Rohingya living in Bangladesh, the question is no longer how many repatriation agreements are signed or names verified, but whether any of them will finally open a road home.

None of Rohingyas return, rather more arrive
item.description:
Nine years ago today, Rohingya began streaming into Bangladesh to escape the genocide in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. In the weeks following 25 August, 2017, more than 700,000 Rohingya fled across the border.

Over this long period, not a single Rohingya has been successfully repatriated to Myanmar. Instead, more than 154,000 additional Rohingya have joined the influx over the past year and a half. At present, more than 1.4 million registered and unregistered Rohingya are living in 33 camps in Ukhiya and Teknaf.

Local representatives and Rohingya leaders say the camps, densely populated and surrounded by hills, have become more than shelters for displaced people. Taking advantage of prolonged uncertainty, unemployment and endless frustration, they have turned into a hub of serious criminal activity.

A total of 292 murders have taken place in the camps over the past nine years. Local communities are increasingly caught in the grip of more than 10 Rohingya armed groups seeking to establish dominance through targeted killings, abductions, drug and arms trafficking, and hostage-taking for ransom.

The impact of this criminal activity is not confined to the camps. It has also cast a deep shadow over local Bangladeshi communities and development partners.

The unchecked activities of criminal networks inside the camps have made life increasingly unsafe for ordinary residents of Ukhiya and Teknaf. Travelling on roads around the camps at night has become risky for local people.

More than 50 local and international NGO officials and employees involved in refugee services are also facing serious security concerns. Fearing for their lives and facing threats from extortionists, NGO workers are being forced to leave the camp areas before 4pm. This is having a negative impact on humanitarian assistance operations in the long run.

Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner (RRRC) Additional Secretary Mohammad Mizanur Rahman said targeted killings and criminal activities by armed groups from Myanmar had increased in the camps.

Joint forces are conducting ongoing operations against the militants. Almost every day, suspects are being arrested with weapons. However, the crisis cannot be fully resolved until the Rohingya are ensured a dignified return to their homeland in Rakhine, he said.

Killings and struggles for dominance

Four major armed groups from Myanmar, along with five or six smaller groups, are currently active in the camps. Their primary objectives are to maintain control over the camps, keep routes for yaba, crystal methamphetamine and arms operational, and profit financially.

Government statistics show that over the past nine years, 15,137 Rohingya have been accused in 5,603 cases filed in the camps. But despite the growing number of cases, the bloodshed has not stopped.

Police and Rohingya leaders say at least 23 people, including commanders from both sides, have been killed in at least 19 major clashes over the past two years, driven by struggles for dominance and internal conflicts.

292 killed in nine years

An analysis of the pattern of crime in the camps from 2017 through 2026 reveals a disturbing picture. Although a degree of order prevailed during the first year after the Rohingya influx began in August 2017, internal conflicts among Rohingya armed groups emerged the following year, when 23 people were killed. In 2019, as drug trafficking—particularly yaba—and struggles for dominance among criminal groups intensified, the number of killings rose to 32.

Even during the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, crime did not not stop; 16 people were killed that year. On the night of 29 September, 2021, Muhibullah, a top Rohingya leader and chairman of the Arakan Rohingya Society for Peace and Human Rights (ARSPH), was shot dead by members of the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA). The following day, six teachers and students at a madrasa were killed. A total of 30 people were killed that year.

As extortion and abductions became widespread in 2022, the number of killings rose to 44. The year 2023 was the bloodiest in the history of the camps, with 83 people killed in unprecedented clashes between ARSA and the Rohingya Solidarity Organisation (RSO) over control of the camps.

Twenty-two people were killed in 2024, 30 the following year, and 12 have been killed through 20 August this year. According to government records, the total number of people killed over the past nine years stands at 292.

However, local representatives and Rohingya leaders say many cases of abduction and murder never result in formal cases because bodies are often hidden out of fear or in remote, dark areas of the hills following killings. They estimate that the actual number of people killed over the past nine years is likely to exceed 325.

After investigating and analysing the crimes, law enforcement agencies say the nature of criminal activity has changed dramatically. It is no longer limited to extortion; child abductions and ransom demands using modern mobile banking services such as bKash and Nagad have also increased.

Abdul Shukkur, president of the Cox’s Bazar branch of the human rights organisation Human Rights Defenders Forum and a senior lawyer, said the failure to repatriate even a single Rohingya over the past nine years had created extreme frustration.

Unless the criminal empires built by armed groups emerging from this frustration are dismantled, the Cox’s Bazar region will face long-term risks, he said.

He added that, alongside strict administrative and military operations, the international community must step up diplomatic efforts to open the way for sustainable repatriation as quickly as possible. This, he said, is the only way to break free from the cycle of bloodshed and crime.

item.title: 17 diplomatic missions, EU say Rohingya repatriation conditions remain unsafe
item.description:
Seventeen diplomatic missions and the European Union have issued a joint statement marking nine years since the mass displacement of Rohingyas from Myanmar, calling for continued international support for the displaced population and saying conditions are not yet in place for their safe and sustainable repatriation.

The joint statement was published on Monday by the Embassy of France in Dhaka.

The signatories include Canada, Denmark, the European Union, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Kosovo, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom.

The statement read, "Nine years after the mass displacement of Rohingya from Myanmar, nearly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh. On this anniversary, we pay tribute to the resilience, courage and dignity of Rohingya communities in the face of ongoing displacement and hardship. We also express our gratitude to the Government and people of Bangladesh for their generosity in providing refuge for nearly a decade."

Rohingya refugees have a right to return to their homes in Myanmar. Regrettably, conflict is escalating across Rakhine and humanitarian need is rising. Deepening insecurity, airstrikes on civilian infrastructure and the Myanmar authorities’ blockades on aid and trade are worsening the humanitarian crisis. This instability is driving further displacement into Bangladesh and across the region, leading to tragic loss of life through dangerous sea crossings, it added.

These conditions do not currently allow for voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable repatriation, said the statement. Creating the conditions for return will require a strategic, coordinated and long-term approach to address the root causes of displacement, build trust between communities, and support greater peace and stability in Myanmar. Successful repatriation will also require equipping Rohingya with the education and skills they will need to rebuild their homes, livelihoods and communities in Rakhine, said the statement.

"We will continue to work with Bangladesh to find pathways towards building the conditions for repatriation. Until then, we remain committed to supporting Rohingya in Bangladesh and the communities who host them, including through strengthening their self-reliance," said the statement.

"The future of the Rohingya response depends not only on sustaining humanitarian assistance, but on improving how it is delivered. We support efforts to strengthen local leadership and increase the role of Bangladeshi and refugee-led actors in shaping and delivering assistance. Rohingya voices must be at the centre of decisions that affect their lives and futures," it added.

The joint statement also said, "As this crisis enters its tenth year, we must ensure that the Rohingya people are not forgotten. We will continue to amplify the voices of Rohingya communities, pursue justice and accountability, and work with Bangladesh and international partners to sustain global support."
